summary: Some middleboxes block IKE negotiation over UDP, which breaks IPsec VPNs. This document describes sending both IKE messages and the encapsulated IPsec packets over a TCP connection so they can pass through. It was replaced by RFC 9329.

eli5.summary: Some gates only let one kind of truck through. This puts your VPN traffic inside that kind of truck so it can still get to the other side.

questions: how to run ikev2 and ipsec over tcp
ipsec over tcp when udp blocked
subtitle: Send IKE and IPsec packets through TCP when UDP is blocked by middleboxes.

tldr.problem: Many network middleboxes (firewalls, proxies on hotspots) block all UDP traffic but allow TCP connections, preventing IPsec VPN negotiation and operation. Devices behind such networks cannot establish secure connections.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 8229 defines a method to encapsulate both IKE control messages and ESP data packets in a TCP connection, with a length field and stream prefix to mark the start of the encapsulated stream.
tldr.outcome: VPN clients can now establish IPsec connections on networks that block UDP, though at the cost of TCP's reliability and ordering overhead. This was replaced by RFC 9329.

today: RFC 8229 is a Proposed Standard for TCP encapsulation of IKE and IPsec packets. It was replaced by RFC 9329.

sections.title: The Problem and Solution
sections.content:
IKEv2 (Internet Key Exchange Protocol version 2) normally uses UDP for negotiating IPsec Security Associations, and IPsec uses UDP port 4500 for encapsulated packets when NAT is detected. Many public networks filter all UDP traffic, allowing only TCP connections that appear to be web traffic. Devices behind such networks cannot establish IPsec VPNs. RFC 8229 solves this by allowing IKE and IPsec packets to be sent over a TCP connection instead, as a fallback when UDP is blocked.

Direct ESP (IP protocol 50) is preferred, then UDP port 4500 encapsulation, then this TCP method. TCP is slower due to in-order delivery and reliability overhead, so implementations should prefer the earlier options when possible.
sections.eli5: Your secure connection tool normally sends traffic as independent packages (UDP), but some networks only allow the kind of traffic used for web pages (TCP). This method converts your security packages into web-like messages so they get through.

sections.title: TCP Encapsulation Format
sections.content:
Each IKE or ESP packet sent over TCP is prefixed with a 16-bit length field in network byte order. For IKE messages, the packet begins with a non-ESP marker (four zero bytes) to distinguish them from ESP packets. For ESP messages, the length field is followed directly by the ESP header.

A TCP stream begins with the magic value IKETCP (ASCII bytes 0x49 0x4B 0x45 0x54 0x43 0x50) sent only once by the TCP Originator (the side that initiates the connection). This identifies the stream as using this protocol and prevents confusion with other non-standard protocols that may have used TCP port 4500.
sections.eli5: Each message is labeled with its size, so the receiver knows where one message ends and the next begins. All messages start with a magic word to prove they are the right kind of traffic.

sections.title: Setting Up and Tearing Down the Connection
sections.content:
The TCP Originator initiates a TCP connection to the Responder on a configured port (default 4500). The first bytes sent MUST be the stream prefix. After that, the Originator sends encapsulated IKE messages to negotiate an IKE SA and Child SA. Once the SA is established, both IKE and ESP packets flow over the same connection.

When closing, either side SHOULD gracefully delete the IKE SA with DELETE payloads. The TCP Originator should close the TCP connection if it no longer needs it. If the connection breaks unexpectedly, the Originator is responsible for re-establishing it. A new connection MUST start with the stream prefix again.
sections.eli5: The connection starts with the magic word, then the two sides negotiate keys like usual, then data flows through. When closing, they say goodbye and shut the connection cleanly.

sections.title: When to Use TCP Encapsulation
sections.content:
RFC 8229 recommends that implementations attempt IKE negotiation over UDP (port 500 and 4500) first. Only after IKE retransmission timers expire should the implementation fall back to TCP encapsulation. Some implementations may use TCP encapsulation on networks known to block UDP. Since TCP encapsulation support is not negotiated in the IKE exchange, both sides must be pre-configured to support it.

The Responder implementation should listen on the configured TCP port(s) for incoming TCP connections from peers configured to use TCP encapsulation. This configuration prevents accidental interoperability problems.
sections.eli5: Try the normal fast way first. Only switch to TCP if the normal way times out or if you know the network blocks UDP.

sections.title: Security and Performance Trade-offs
sections.content:
TCP encapsulation introduces new risks: TCP responders become vulnerable to SYN-flooding DoS attacks specific to TCP, and spurious TCP Reset packets can disrupt the connection. However, implementations can keep IKE session state persistent across TCP connection breaks. Since TCP provides in-order delivery, ESP implementations SHOULD set the anti-replay window to 1, reducing the risk of replay attacks.

Performance suffers because TCP-in-TCP causes nested congestion control problems: packet loss on the outer TCP is hidden from inner flows as delay, potentially causing spurious retransmissions and reduced throughput. Real-time traffic like Voice over IP is negatively impacted when mixed with general traffic through a single TCP tunnel.
sections.eli5: Using TCP is safer for some attacks but slower because TCP tries to deliver everything reliably, which creates problems when you have two layers of TCP fighting each other.

sections.title: NAT Detection and Mobility
sections.content: IKE_SA_INIT messages sent over TCP include NAT_DETECTION_SOURCE_IP and NAT_DETECTION_DESTINATION_IP payloads (computed using TCP ports), though TCP encapsulation already handles NAT traversal inherently. If MOBIKE (IKEv2 Mobility and Multihoming) is in use, peers can switch between TCP encapsulation and UDP encapsulation as they move between networks. The Originator should first try UPDATE_SA_ADDRESSES over UDP; if the Responder only responds over TCP, the connection switches to TCP.
sections.eli5: The system can detect if there is a NAT in the path and can switch from UDP to TCP or back if you move to a different network.
